newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Dematerialised Minfins may settle freeze problems.
newsitem.headline: Dematerialised Minfins may settle freeze problems.

text.p: The problem of frozen Russian MinFin bonds could be resolved by observing current civil laws, while dematerialisation of bonds would prevent such cases in future, a top Vneshtorgbank official told Reuters.
"There is a contradiction between criminal and civil legislation," Alexander Osiptsev, vice-chairman responsible for securities operations, said.
"Police may freeze stolen bonds, but civil law prohibits violations of the rights of buyers in good faith."
Vneshtorgbank is the main depositary for MinFin bonds.

A Moscow district prosecutor's office issued an order to freeze $56.81 million face value in June. The bonds were frozen as part of an investigation into the head of a small bank which has since closed.

This would bring the total bonds currently known to have been frozen to $74 million, including around $24 million already detailed by the finance ministry in July, some of which had been stolen in the breakaway republic of Chechnya.
Owners of previously frozen MinFins have not received coupon payments.
The MinFin bond market has been less liquid since last Monday when rumours first circulated about the further seizures.
Osiptsev said that freeze was done last week in the presence of clients and prosecutor office officials.
Some clients refused to sign the protocol of freezing.
"If in summer investors were at a loss what to do, now they are confident they will be able to defend their rights in a state governed by the rule of law," he said.

"It is not clear how property which cannot be withdrawn from the current owner without a court's decision can be seized. The Rights of a buyer of bearer bonds in good faith can be disputed only in court."

He added the problem was overshadowing Russia's Eurobond issue, expected this month. But the impact was purely psychological, because Eurobonds will be non-cash, will have no individual numbers and be clearable through Euroclear and CEDEL.
Vneshtorgbank has around $38 million face value of recently frozen MinFins in its depositary, the official said. The rest are in other depositaries or held directly by owners.
The bank has around 70 percent of the whole $11 billion MinFin bond issue in its depositary, the official said.
As a depositary, Vneshtorgbank was obliged to stop trading in recently frozen MinFins and block further circulation.
Osiptsev said the best way to avoid such problems in future is dematerialisation of the MinFin bond market.
"The finance ministry and central bank are more attentive to the problem now. We hope the government will finally issue the decree or something like this by the end of 1996," he said.
He added the central bank had proposed that Vneshtorgbank set up in its depositary a depersonalised form of custody without waiting for dematerialisation.

"Our clients would forget about specific bonds, but the main problem is the way of sharing risks among all for such cases of freezing. A lesser problem is getting every one of our 700 odd clients to accept it," he said.
He added another way would be for dealers to confirm the serial number of each bond on every deal, but this would be impractical, given the huge amount of deals struck daily.
"If dematerialisation is approved, we will get rid of some 40 percent of the headache because it will be a normal clearing, with only money sums moving," he said.
"There is a hunger for Russian debt, people are waiting for the time when they can invest in Russia in relative safety".
--Moscow newsroom (095) 941 8520
